routes.description: Build a cumulative historical inference from early resurrection testimony, the unexpected individual-resurrection claim, Christianity's worldwide expansion, and later cross-cultural visions to Jesus's historical resurrection.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the relevant phenomena are historically supported, resist the principal ordinary and comparative explanations, and jointly make an actual resurrection a plausible explanation of the motion's full evidential pattern.

motionBridge.description: Show why the combined pattern of early appearances, unexpected messianic interpretation, worldwide expansion, and later visions points to Jesus actually rising from the dead.

centralBridges.description: Establish that early and multiple appearance testimony provides historically significant support for encounters with the risen Jesus.
Show that available Jewish expectations do not adequately explain the emergence of the claim that one crucified Messiah had already bodily risen.
Connect Christianity's exceptional expansion and fulfillment of Jesus's stated worldwide mission to the continuing activity of the risen Jesus.
Show that recurring visions of Jesus, especially among non-Christians who convert, are distinctive evidence of continuing risen activity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Identify relevant differences between the resurrection evidence and allegedly comparable testimony from other religious traditions.
Explain why each evidential line contributes as part of a cumulative case even if no single line independently establishes resurrection.

routes.description: Show that critical historical inquiry cannot infer a physical resurrection from indirect appearance reports, psychologically and socially explicable belief formation, religious growth, or recurring vision traditions.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the offered phenomena remain compatible with ordinary testimonial, perceptual, psychological, social, or comparative religious explanations, leaving resurrection insufficiently established as a historical conclusion.

motionBridge.description: Show that the admissible historical evidence does not overcome ordinary explanations or the probability problem posed by an otherwise unprecedented return from death.

centralBridges.description: Establish that most named appearance claims are indirectly reported and must be tested by the same reliability standards applied to comparable religious testimony.
Explain how perceived postmortem experiences, prior knowledge, psychology, Jewish afterlife concepts, and social reinforcement could generate resurrection belief.
Show that Christianity's influence and expansion demonstrate conviction or institutional success without identifying a miraculous historical cause.
Show that dreams and later visions neither establish the reality of their objects nor uniquely distinguish Christianity from other religious traditions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use structurally comparable witness, miracle, growth, and vision traditions to test whether the affirmative applies its evidential criteria impartially.
Maintain the distinction between theological interpretation and the source criticism and probability judgments required for a historical conclusion.

sections.title: Early Appearance Testimony and Source Reliability
sections.rationale: This issue tests the historical basis of the earliest appearance claims, including direct versus indirect testimony, multiplicity, accessibility, and consistent treatment of comparable religious witnesses.

sections.title: Unexpected Messianic Claim and Formation of Resurrection Belief
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether an individual risen Messiah was too unexpected to arise naturally or could emerge from visionary experiences, Jewish afterlife concepts, and communal reinforcement.

sections.title: Ordinary Explanations and Historical Probability
sections.rationale: This issue examines bereavement experiences, mistaken perception, Paul's conversion, cumulative inference, physical regularities, and the evidential standard for establishing resurrection historically.

sections.title: Christianity's Expansion, Influence, and Fulfilled Mission
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether Christianity's worldwide growth and Jesus's exceptional influence support continuing risen activity or merely record the later success of a religious movement.

sections.title: Later Visions and Comparative Religious Experience
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether cross-cultural visions of Jesus provide distinctive continuing evidence or remain nondiagnostic alongside dreams, healings, and vision traditions found in other religions.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Early Pauline material transmits traditions about Jesus's crucifixion, resurrection claims, and appearances that Bass treats as bedrock sources for a cumulative historical case.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly hands the positive case to Justin Bass, who then presents his book's bedrock framework continuously.

response.rationale: This constructive move identifies the early Pauline resurrection and appearance traditions that ground the affirmative's first evidential line.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly establishes the proposed source foundation, though it compresses the sources' reliability and independence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The bedrock-source proposition is recoverable, but the scope and historical force of the grouped Pauline traditions remain only implicitly qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The sources are specifically identified, but describing the underlying idea as unparalleled outruns the limited comparative support presented here.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The identified traditions can coherently supply data for a cumulative case, although the bridge from early tradition to historical occurrence remains implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: First Corinthians 15 supplies specific support, but dating, transmission, independence, and reliability are asserted more than defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, this directly supplies the early-source foundation for the appearance bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily constructs an evidential foundation and does not meaningfully test a live opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bass names crucifixion, the resurrection claim, and appearances catalogued in First Corinthians 15 as early bedrock material.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: The reported appearances provide cumulative testimony for resurrection because they include multiple claims presented as early and historically accessible evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Justin about the appearances, and Bass answers at length using Paul and the appearance tradition as his evidence.

response.rationale: This constructive move develops the affirmative's appearance line by presenting multiple early claims, including Paul's claimed hostile encounter, as cumulative testimony.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it adds a material testimonial line but leaves accessibility, independence, and corroboration substantially compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative-testimony claim is clear, while the extent to which the reports are multiple independent and accessible testimonies is not fully specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Bass uses probabilistic language, but the historical weight assigned to reported appearances exceeds the source analysis supplied in this span.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Multiple appearance claims can contribute cumulatively, but multiplicity alone does not establish independence or accurate perception.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Paul's own claimed experience is concrete support, while the other reports' directness, independence, and verification remain materially underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, the move directly advances the historically significant early-appearances bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances affirmative evidence without developing or evaluating a sufficiently defined competing account.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bass presents the appearances as evidence Paul could offer and emphasizes Paul's claim that Jesus appeared to him despite his prior hostility.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Only Paul's experience is directly self-attested, while the other named appearance reports rest on indirect sources requiring ordinary historical reliability analysis.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator requests Bart Ehrman's degree of agreement, and Ehrman answers by distinguishing Paul's testimony from reports about other alleged witnesses.

components.text: Whether the multiple appearance claims constitute historically accessible and reliable testimony rather than merely reported claims.
Whether the Pauline bedrock material provides direct sources for all of the named appearance experiences.

response.rationale: Ehrman directly limits the testimonial foundation by distinguishing Paul's self-report from indirect reports and invokes comparable religious experience reports as a reliability check.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it contacts the decisive source-status problem explicitly, though it does not examine every named report separately.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between Paul's direct self-attestation and indirect reports concerning others is clear and expressly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move makes a limited source-critical claim and acknowledges experiences while withholding conclusions that the evidence cannot establish.

charity.alternative: The early Christian reports may preserve genuine experiences even when they are not first-person accounts.
charity.decisiveQualification: Preservation of a report does not make it direct testimony or establish the reported experience's reliability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from indirect reporting to a need for ordinary reliability analysis is explicit, consistent, and appropriately limited.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The direct-versus-indirect distinction is specific and relevant, though the excerpt does not document each underlying source in detail.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, the move directly supplies the source-and-testimony limitation required by the skeptical route.

representationalCharity.rationale: Ehrman grants that reported religious experiences may have occurred while accurately preserving the source-critical qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman distinguishes belief that someone had an experience from proof of its object and compares Christian reports with reports in other traditions.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Historical inquiry cannot privilege Christian appearance sources while rejecting comparable non-Christian eyewitness claims that satisfy the same proposed testimonial criteria.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman controls the main argumentative thread while Bass briefly interjects about authorship and the number of Christian sources.

components.text: Whether the proposed testimonial criteria are applied consistently to comparable Christian and non-Christian appearance claims.
Whether calling selected Christian sources bedrock improperly privileges sources that support the affirmative conclusion.

response.rationale: Ehrman contacts the affirmative source claims by demanding impartial historical evaluation rather than accepting favorable sources because they support Christianity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it directly states the methodological challenge, but the interrupted span leaves the comparison's examples and criteria compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The impartiality demand is clear, though the relevant class of comparable claims and exact acceptance criteria are only partly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Requiring consistent source evaluation is proportionate to the methodological claim, with only the comparison set left implicit.

charity.alternative: Christian sources might be preferred because they differ in date, number, independence, or contextual fit.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those differences must be demonstrated rather than inferred from agreement with the preferred conclusion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The consistency principle follows cleanly, although equal standards do not by themselves imply equal evidential outcomes.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The methodological warrant is strong, but representative non-Christian cases and detailed criterion-by-criterion comparison are not supplied here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, this strongly advances the comparative-religious-claims bridge through an impartiality test.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move allows source evaluation in principle but does not fully discuss potentially relevant distinctions among the traditions.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman states that historians evaluate sources rather than prove a faith and criticizes accepting sources merely because they agree with one's view.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Unexpected resurrection belief could arise from initial experiences interpreted as sightings of Jesus and then spread through subsequent communal claims and social reinforcement without an actual resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: After the moderator clarifies Bass's unexpectedness argument, Ehrman explicitly accepts the clarification and presents his alternative account.

components.text: Whether an unexpected resurrection claim requires an actual resurrection rather than experiences interpreted and socially transmitted afterward.
Whether the reported multiplicity discloses independent experiences or later claims spreading after initial perceived appearances.

response.rationale: Ehrman accepts that resurrection was not expected and directly offers an alternative pathway from perceived sightings to additional claims and communal belief.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the unexpectedness inference and supplies the defeating consequence that unexpected belief can still arise naturally.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed sequence from perceived experiences to subsequent claims is recoverable and repeatedly qualified as uncertain about who experienced what.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Ehrman distinguishes probable and certain individual cases from unknown cases and presents the pathway as an explanation rather than certainty.

charity.alternative: The followers did not expect resurrection and may sincerely have believed that Jesus physically appeared.
charity.decisiveQualification: Sincerity and prior unexpectedness do not determine whether the perceived appearances had a resurrected external object.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The causal pathway is coherent and answers the unexpectedness inference, though the social-reinforcement stages remain somewhat compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The pathway fits acknowledged claims and uncertainty, but its psychological and transmission mechanisms receive little specific documentation in this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly advances the natural-belief-formation bridge with an explicit alternative pathway.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move expressly grants both unexpectedness and sincere perceived sightings before denying that they uniquely establish resurrection.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman says Peter and Mary probably, and Paul certainly, thought they saw Jesus, while stressing uncertainty about others and later claims.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Apocalyptic Jewish beliefs about embodied afterlife explain why followers who thought they saw Jesus alive could infer that God had bodily raised him.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator prompts the historical reconstruction, and Ehrman gives a sustained explanation grounded in the followers' prior apocalyptic Jewish worldview.

components.text: Whether Jewish conceptual resources could convert a perceived postmortem sighting into a bodily-resurrection claim.
Whether interpretation of perceived appearances depends on the followers' prior embodied-afterlife framework.

response.rationale: Ehrman directly supplies the missing interpretive bridge: apocalyptic Jews who conceived afterlife bodily could infer resurrection from believing they saw Jesus alive.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly addresses how the unexpected bodily claim could arise, though its generalization about Jewish belief is broad.

precisionFindings.rationale: The embodied-inference proposition is clear, but statements about what apocalyptic Jews could imagine are broader than the evidence presented warrants.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical claim that embodied existence was the only imaginable afterlife overstates what the excerpt establishes about diverse Jewish views.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If the stated apocalyptic premises hold, the inference to bodily raising is coherent; the breadth of those premises is the main limitation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A relevant Jewish conceptual framework is identified, but its asserted uniformity and exclusivity lack representative support in the presented evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, this directly provides an interpretive mechanism for natural formation of bodily-resurrection belief.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move mainly constructs a historical interpretive mechanism and does not substantially evaluate a developed competing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman argues that apocalyptic Jews treated embodied existence as the available afterlife category, shaping interpretation of seeing Jesus alive.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Jewish categories permitted exalted heavenly existence followed by resurrection at the end, but did not naturally yield the claim that Jesus had already risen bodily.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator requests a quick response, and Bass presents the Jewish alternatives before directly challenging Ehrman's reconstruction of innovation.

components.text: Whether Jewish embodied-afterlife categories naturally explain the unprecedented claim that one person had risen before the final resurrection.
Whether perceived sightings plus Jewish categories adequately explain the timing and specific content of the immediate claim.

response.rationale: Bass directly distinguishes heavenly survival and end-time resurrection from the early Christian claim that Jesus had already bodily risen, challenging the proposed conceptual pathway.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it contacts the decisive timing distinction explicitly but does not show why innovation from existing categories was implausible.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast among heavenly exaltation, final resurrection, and Jesus's claimed immediate resurrection is clear, with comparative scope only implicitly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The distinction is evidentially relevant, but its ability to exclude conceptual innovation or reinterpretation is stronger than the supplied warrant.

charity.alternative: Existing embodied-resurrection expectations could be adapted after followers believed that they saw Jesus alive.
charity.decisiveQualification: The adaptation would still need to explain the novel claim that one Messiah had risen before the general resurrection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The categorical distinction creates a genuine explanatory demand, but novelty alone does not entail that ordinary belief formation is inadequate.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Maccabean and final-resurrection contrast is concrete, while the breadth of Jewish expectations and innovation mechanisms remain underdocumented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly attacks the skeptical natural-belief-formation account's embodied-inference step.

representationalCharity.rationale: Bass identifies the strongest conceptual pathway and isolates its timing problem, though he does not fully examine mechanisms of innovation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bass contrasts martyrs living exalted in heaven until the final resurrection with the Christian assertion that Jesus had already risen now.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Reports of postmortem appearances do not disclose what most witnesses actually experienced and therefore remain compatible with multiple ordinary explanations.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly solicits Ehrman's account, and the sustained first-person answer matches his previously stated skeptical position.

components.text: Whether the appearance reports reveal what the alleged witnesses experienced well enough to establish resurrection over ordinary options.
Whether the early source base contains first-person descriptions sufficient to identify the appearances' cause.
Whether a novel interpretation resolves the underlying uncertainty about what was actually perceived.

response.rationale: Ehrman directly argues that the sources usually do not disclose what witnesses saw and therefore support options rather than a determinate miraculous conclusion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive evidential-underdetermination component but does not address the separate unexpectedness argument.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is carefully limited to what can be known from sparse reports and explicitly allows multiple possible explanations.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move expressly emphasizes uncertainty, options, and the limited first-person record rather than asserting one speculative explanation as certain.

charity.alternative: Several people may genuinely have had experiences that they understood as encounters with the living Jesus.
charity.decisiveQualification: Genuine experiences and sincere interpretation do not identify their cause when descriptions and direct testimony are sparse.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Limited direct descriptions rationally entail underdetermination among causal options, without requiring denial that experiences occurred.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The claim is tied to the paucity of first-person testimony, although a fuller source-by-source demonstration is not included here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the motion tier, it directly advances historical insufficiency by showing that the central appearance evidence underdetermines resurrection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument grants possible experiences and focuses fairly on the narrower historical inability to determine their content and cause.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman says historians can often only identify options because witnesses do not tell what they saw, with Paul the sole direct claimant identified.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: An ordinary bereavement-vision explanation does not readily account for Paul, an enemy of the Christian movement, experiencing Jesus and converting.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly challenges Bart's recurring-vision analogy and presses him for a documented case involving an enemy apparition.

components.text: Whether familiar postmortem or projected-apparition explanations plausibly cover Paul's hostile pre-conversion situation.
Whether the proposed natural pathway supplies a specific mechanism for Paul's experience and conversion.

response.rationale: Bass challenges the ordinary-experience account with Paul's hostility and demands a comparable enemy-apparition case; Ehrman's interjected guilt hypothesis leaves the exchange unresolved.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts a decisive difficult case for the natural account but does not establish that no ordinary mechanism applies.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge concerning Paul is clear, but 'enemy apparition' compresses several possible psychological or perceptual mechanisms into one label.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Bass frames the point as a challenge and request for examples rather than claiming deductive exclusion of all ordinary accounts.

charity.alternative: Guilt, conflict, or other psychological mechanisms could produce an experience involving a perceived enemy.
charity.decisiveQualification: A general possibility still needs case-specific evidence connecting such a mechanism to Paul.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Paul's prior hostility is a relevant challenge to simple bereavement models, but it does not exhaust other natural mechanisms.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Paul's hostile posture is concrete evidence, while the rarity of such visions and its psychological significance are not documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it materially attacks the skeptical natural-belief-formation bridge using its hardest individual case.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move permits the natural account to answer with examples but narrows it somewhat through the compressed 'enemy apparition' framing.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bass asks where people project apparitions of enemies and invokes Paul; Ehrman answers that guilt can sometimes produce such experiences.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Historical probability favors familiar mistaken perception or testimony over a uniquely reported event that conflicts with consistently observed physical regularities.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker states his disbelief in resurrection, invokes physical law, and then explicitly frames the issue through historians' probability judgments.

components.text: Whether difficulty explaining Paul's experience makes resurrection the most probable historical explanation.
Whether testimony from Paul and Peter overcomes the prior improbability associated with an unprecedented physical event.
Whether the claim's singular novelty supports rather than reduces its historical probability.

response.rationale: Ehrman identifies the inferential failure directly: limited testimony and gaps in ordinary reconstruction do not make violation of uniformly observed physical regularities the most probable event.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it expressly identifies the probability mismatch and states the consequence for the proposed historical inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The probability challenge is clear, but calling resurrection a violation of a law of physics leaves the relevant law and divine-causation qualification imprecise.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Uniform observed mortality strongly supports the probability challenge, but the categorical cosmological formulation exceeds what historical observation strictly establishes.

charity.alternative: If God exists and has reason to raise Jesus, resurrection need not have the ordinary physical base rate.
charity.decisiveQualification: The historical evidence offered must independently justify those theological priors rather than assume them in estimating probability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The base-rate objection coherently defeats an inference from unexplained testimony to most-probable resurrection, despite an overstated physics formulation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Consistent observation that dead people remain dead gives strong representative support, with the divine-action prior left comparatively underexamined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the motion tier, this directly contests whether the affirmative evidence can overcome the central historical-probability problem.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly challenges the historical inference but compresses the affirmative's potential background-theology response into physical regularity.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman contrasts Paul and Peter's reports with the otherwise uniform physical history of death and challenges calling resurrection most probable.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: The appearance evidence is consistent with Jesus having risen and contributes to a broader cumulative case rather than being offered as the sole proof of resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker distinguishes the appearance material from additional forthcoming evidence and cites Ehrman's own treatment of the evidentiary fit.

components.text: Whether appearance evidence must independently make resurrection most probable or may contribute within a broader cumulative explanation.
Whether consistency with resurrection supplies positive evidential weight despite underdetermination by appearances alone.

response.rationale: Bass directly narrows the claim: appearances are not sole proof but are consistent with resurrection and form one line in a broader cumulative case.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the demand that appearances alone overcome probability but postpones the needed comparative cumulative warrant.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly states the limited role of appearances and explicitly denies that this evidential line is the only evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A claim of consistency and cumulative contribution is appropriately modest, although consistency alone supplies limited discriminatory force.

charity.alternative: Appearance evidence may be consistent with resurrection while also fitting several ordinary explanations.
charity.decisiveQualification: Its cumulative value depends on comparative likelihood, not mere compatibility with the affirmative hypothesis.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cumulative framing is coherent, but the move leaves the crucial bridge from compatibility to incremental evidential support largely implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The cited concession supports consistency, not a favorable comparison against ordinary explanations or the full cumulative inference.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the motion tier, it directly attempts to answer historical insufficiency by reframing the inference as cumulative.

representationalCharity.rationale: Bass acknowledges that appearances are not sufficient alone but does not squarely address the strongest nondiagnostic-consistency objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bass says the appearances are not the only evidence and invokes Ehrman's statement that the evidence is consistent with Jesus having risen.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Jesus's singular worldwide worship as Lord and God is an extraordinary historical anomaly that Bass offers as relevant context for assessing the singular resurrection claim.
moves.attributionBasis: Bass takes the floor after the moderator's invitation, repeatedly identifies the worship of Jesus as his anomaly, and links it to resurrection.

components.text: Whether the singularity of the alleged resurrection lacks correspondingly singular historical context that could affect its assessment.
Whether later worldwide worship supplies information capable of resolving the early appearance evidence's underdetermination.

response.rationale: Bass answers the singular-event objection by identifying Jesus's worldwide divine worship as a singular contextual anomaly, but does not establish the causal connection to resurrection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive singularity concern but leaves the bridge from later worship to resurrection probability undeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The worldwide-worship claim is recoverable, but 'one human being' and the global comparison class are broad and insufficiently qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The extraordinary scale of worship is relevant context, but it does not by itself warrant the asserted implication toward a singular miracle.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move identifies an anomaly but leaves a substantial non sequitur between later worldwide worship and Jesus's physical resurrection.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Widespread worship is readily observable in broad terms, but uniqueness, comparison, and miraculous causal relevance are largely asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the motion tier, the move directly attempts to affect the overall resurrection inference through claimed singular context.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move introduces a new contextual anomaly rather than carefully evaluating a developed alternative explanation of that anomaly.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bass cites Jesus as uniquely worshipped by billions as Lord and God and presents that worldwide status as an extraordinary historical anomaly.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The number of people convinced by a resurrection claim demonstrates widespread conviction but does not establish the truth of the alleged miracle.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly distinguishes evidence that people became convinced from evidence that God actually intervened, matching Ehrman's response.

components.text: Whether widespread conviction and worship establish the truth or miraculous cause of the resurrection claim.
Whether adding later conviction to a cumulative case supplies an independent bridge to the alleged miracle.

response.rationale: Ehrman explicitly distinguishes evidence that many became convinced from evidence that the miracle occurred and states that conviction can have other causes.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it precisely identifies the equivocation between widespread belief and truth and gives the defeating consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between evidence of conviction and evidence of the alleged event is explicit, stable, and appropriately scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The logical restriction on what popularity directly establishes is proportionate and does not require uncertainty about the conceptual distinction.

charity.alternative: Large-scale durable conviction might be indirect evidence if miraculous origin predicts it better than ordinary causes.
charity.decisiveQualification: That comparative causal warrant must be shown; the number convinced alone establishes only the belief's spread.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The belief-truth distinction is explicit and directly defeats the inference from many believers to the truth of the miracle.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The point rests on a well-supported inferential distinction, though alternative causes are stated generally rather than illustrated here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly advances the claim that growth and conviction are nondiagnostic of miraculous origin.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move preserves the possibility of other arguments while correctly rejecting conviction itself as proof of miraculous causation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman states that numbers can establish that people became convinced, while people also become convinced for reasons other than divine intervention.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Christianity's early growth rate is naturally reproducible, as comparable religious growth demonstrates, and therefore does not identify a miraculous origin.
moves.attributionBasis: Ehrman introduces the numerical comparison with Mormon growth and expressly concludes that growth does not indicate miraculous beginnings.

components.text: Whether exceptional Christian scale or growth identifies a miraculous beginning rather than reproducible movement dynamics.
Whether movement growth supplies an independent cumulative evidential line for resurrection.

response.rationale: Ehrman attacks the causal inference by invoking comparable growth and explaining that stable early growth rates can yield large populations without miraculous origins.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it states why growth is nondiagnostic and supplies a comparative and mathematical consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition concerns what growth rates can establish and is clearly distinguished from denying that Christianity actually grew.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited conclusion that growth does not identify miraculous beginnings fits the comparative and compounding-growth warrant.

charity.alternative: Christian growth may still be unusual in duration, reach, content, or historical influence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those features require comparative causal analysis and cannot make growth rate alone evidence of miraculous origin.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparison and compounding-growth point coherently show why large eventual scale does not uniquely identify an initial miracle.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A concrete growth-rate consequence and comparative religious case support the claim, with detailed empirical rate documentation omitted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly and strongly advances the growth-nondiagnostic bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move addresses the strongest scale inference while leaving room for more discriminating comparative features to be argued.

moves.evidenceBasis: Ehrman notes comparable religious growth and observes that extending Christianity's early growth rate would exceed the world's population.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Christianity's worldwide expansion fulfills the objective attributed to the risen Jesus and therefore supports Bass's claim that Jesus continued directing the church.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly yields to Justin, and the sustained first-person presentation matches Justin's resurrection defense throughout the exchange.

response.rationale: This constructive move connects Christianity's worldwide expansion with an objective attributed to Jesus and treats fulfillment as evidence of continuing direction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it identifies the proposed fulfillment bridge but leaves attribution, prediction specificity, and causal discrimination underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The mission-fulfillment proposition is recoverable, but 'we know what he wanted' and continuing direction have unstable historical and theological scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Worldwide expansion is relevant to fulfillment, but the excerpt does not warrant confident attribution to the risen Jesus's continuing activity.

charity.alternative: The New Testament may attribute a worldwide mission to Jesus even if the sayings are later community formulations.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical fulfillment evidence depends on independent dating and attribution rather than accepting the narrative's theological framing.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If an independently established prediction and continuing agency were shown, fulfillment could matter; those central bridges remain largely assumed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Christianity's spread is evident, but historical attribution of the objective, prediction specificity, and supernatural causation lack developed support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, the move directly targets expansion and fulfilled mission as evidence of continuing risen activity.

representationalCharity.rationale: Bass briefly acknowledges dispute over risen-Jesus sayings but then proceeds as though the relevant desire is historically known.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bass introduces worldwide mission as a fourth bedrock line and says the New Testament reveals what Jesus, including the risen Jesus, wanted.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Recurring visions of Jesus across cultures and centuries, including reports involving non-Christians who convert, provide an additional line of evidence for continuing risen activity.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator invites Justin's next line of evidence, and Justin identifies his own research project before presenting the sustained argument.

response.rationale: This constructive move presents recurring visions among non-Christians who convert as another evidential line for Jesus's continuing risen activity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it specifies a potentially discriminating cross-cultural phenomenon but relies on unverified reports and a compressed causal inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed phenomenon is clear, while its frequency, population, cultural scope, and definition of a vision are not adequately bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Reports of converting visions may merit inquiry, but the move too quickly attributes them to Jesus's intentional continuing activity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Cross-cultural conversion reports could be relevant, but the bridge from reports to an objectively active risen Jesus remains material and implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies on generalized reports without representative cases, verification standards, base rates, or systematic comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly supplies the later cross-cultural visions line required by the affirmative route.

representationalCharity.rationale: Bass anticipates comparison with other religions but does not yet evaluate a developed comparative explanation in this constructive span.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bass says unbelievers across cultures report visions of Jesus and convert, interpreting this as Jesus continuing to seek and save people.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Dreams do not establish that their perceived objects are real, and comparable vision and healing traditions outside Christianity prevent later Jesus visions from being uniquely diagnostic.
moves.attributionBasis: Justin addresses Bart by name before the reply, and the response's skeptical treatment of dreams and ancient cult testimony clearly belongs to Bart.

components.text: Whether dreams and visions establish the reality of Jesus as their object rather than merely the occurrence of experiences.
Whether recurring religious experiences identify continuing direction of a worldwide mission.
Whether comparable religious vision and healing traditions undermine claimed Christian uniqueness.

response.rationale: Ehrman directly argues that dreams do not validate their objects and cites Asclepius and other traditions to challenge uniqueness, while not addressing mission fulfillment itself.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts both the object-reality and comparative components but does not fully test cross-cultural conversion rates.

precisionFindings.rationale: The nondiagnostic-dream principle is clear, though the asserted breadth and structural comparability of outside traditions are only partly specified.

charity.alternative: Cross-cultural visions followed by conversion may differ from ordinary within-tradition dreams and healing visions.
charity.decisiveQualification: The alleged distinction needs systematic comparative evidence before it can identify the vision's object or supernatural cause.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between having a dream and establishing its object's reality is explicit; the comparative extension has one bounded bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Asclepius supplies a concrete comparative tradition, but representativeness and precise cross-cultural similarity remain underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly advances the visions-nondiagnostic bridge through object-reality and comparative challenges.

representationalCharity.rationale: Ehrman addresses comparable traditions fairly at a structural level but does not fully engage the conversion-across-traditions qualification.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Reports of people from other religious backgrounds seeing Jesus and moving toward Christianity distinguish the offered phenomenon from ordinary visions occurring within a person's own tradition.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator frames this as Justin's attempted historical connection, after which Justin contrasts visions across named religious traditions.

components.text: Whether Christian vision reports differ because people outside Christianity see Jesus and move across religious boundaries.
Whether ordinary social reinforcement explains reports arising among people initially outside Christian communities.
Whether the asserted cross-religious pattern has been established under impartial source standards.

response.rationale: Bass directly proposes cross-religious conversion as a distinction from within-tradition visions, but openly signals uncertainty and offers Google search rather than systematic verification.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive comparative component but leaves impartial verification and counterexamples unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The intended cross-religious distinction is visible, but fragmented wording and categorical geographic claims obscure its actual frequency and scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Bass voices uncertainty about whether the claim is true, yet still calls the pattern amazing and broadly absent elsewhere without adequate warrant.

charity.alternative: Other traditions may include visions crossing religious boundaries, even if many experiences occur within a person's inherited tradition.
charity.decisiveQualification: A distinctive Christian frequency or conversion effect requires systematic comparative evidence, not selected reports or search results.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A verified asymmetry could distinguish the cases, but the move shifts from uncertainty to categorical comparison without a stable evidential bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The broad comparative conclusion rests on assertion and proposed internet searching, without representative data, verification, or rival cases.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly attacks the claim that later visions are nondiagnostic by proposing a cross-religious distinction.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges within-tradition visions but materially weakens the live alternative by asserting cross-boundary absence without substantiation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Bass says people have visions within their own religions but claims cross-religious Jesus visions differ, while admitting uncertainty and invoking Google searches.
